Define Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and each word in the name
Describe the three steps of RAG at question time: retrieve, augment, generate
List two benefits and one limitation of RAG

embedding (a list of numbers that captures the meaning of text)
embedding model (a tool that turns text into embeddings)

analogy.story: A student sits for an open-book exam. The student first looks up the relevant page in the textbook (retrieval), then writes the answer using that page (generation).
analogy.mapping: The textbook is the knowledge base. Looking up the page is retrieval. Writing the answer is generation. The student is the LLM.

worked_example.setting: A college student in Bhopal uses a chatbot on the college website to ask about the new hostel fee.
worked_example.question: What is the hostel fee for first-year B.Sc students this year?
documents: Hostel Fee Notice 2024-25: First-year B.Sc hostel fee is ₹45,000 per year, payable in two instalments.
Hostel Fee Notice 2023-24: First-year B.Sc hostel fee was ₹40,000 per year.
Mess Menu: Monday breakfast is poha and tea.
worked_example.retrieved: Hostel Fee Notice 2024-25: First-year B.Sc hostel fee is ₹45,000 per year, payable in two instalments.
worked_example.answer_without_rag: The hostel fee for first-year B.Sc students is ₹40,000 per year.
worked_example.answer_with_rag: According to the 2024-25 notice, the hostel fee for first-year B.Sc students is ₹45,000 per year, payable in two instalments.

sections.heading: ## What You Will Learn
sections.goal: Give the learner a clear list of what they will be able to do after the lesson.
points: You will explain what a Large Language Model (LLM) is and its limits (F1, F2, F3, F4).
You will define Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and each word in the name (F5).
You will describe the three question-time steps: retrieve, augment, generate (F8).
You will list two benefits and one limitation of RAG (F11, F12).

sections.heading: ## Before We Start: Some Basic Ideas
sections.goal: Introduce AI, LLM, and the three main limits of an LLM.
points: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a computer system that can do tasks that usually need human intelligence.
A Large Language Model (LLM) is an AI model trained on a very large amount of text. It generates text by predicting the next token (a word or part of a word) (F1).
An LLM has a knowledge cutoff: it does not know events after its training date (F2).
An LLM does not know private or organisation-specific information it was never trained on (F3).
An LLM can produce answers that sound confident but are wrong or made up. This is called hallucination (F4).

sections.heading: ## What Is RAG?
sections.goal: Define RAG, give the full form, and explain each word.
points: RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (F5, F6).
Retrieval means finding and fetching relevant pieces of information from an outside source.
Augmented means added to or made stronger: the retrieved text is added to the question in the prompt.
Generation means the LLM writes the answer using the question plus the retrieved context.
RAG does not change or retrain the model. The model's weights stay the same (F9).

sections.heading: ## Why Does RAG Matter?
sections.goal: Explain the benefits of RAG and contrast with fine-tuning.
points: RAG lets the LLM use up-to-date and private information (F11).
RAG reduces made-up answers (hallucinations), though it does not remove them completely (F11).
Answers can show their sources, so users can check (F11).
RAG is cheaper and faster than retraining or fine-tuning the model (F10, F11).
Knowledge is easy to update by changing the documents, not the model (F9, F11).
Fine-tuning trains the model further on new examples and changes its weights. It is slower and costlier, and mainly used to change style or behaviour (F10).

sections.heading: ## How Does RAG Work?
sections.goal: Describe the preparation step and the three question-time steps in order.
points: Preparation (indexing) happens before any question arrives (F7).
Collect the documents, split them into small pieces called chunks (a small piece of a document) (F7).
Turn each chunk into an embedding (a list of numbers that captures the meaning of text) using an embedding model (a tool that turns text into embeddings) (F7).
Store the embeddings in a vector database (a searchable store of vectors) (F7).

Question-time step 1: Retrieve. The user's question is also turned into an embedding. The system finds the chunks whose meaning is most similar (semantic search). Usually the top few (top-k) chunks are taken (F8).
Question-time step 2: Augment. The retrieved chunks are placed into the prompt together with the question and an instruction such as 'answer using only this information' (F8).
Question-time step 3: Generate. The LLM writes the answer from the question plus the retrieved context. It can also cite the sources it used (F8).
Only a limited amount of text fits in the prompt (the context window) (F12).

sections.heading: ## Example: College Hostel Fee Chatbot
sections.goal: Show a concrete Indian example of RAG in action.
points: Setting: A college student in Bhopal uses a chatbot on the college website.
Question: 'What is the hostel fee for first-year B.Sc students this year?'
Documents in the knowledge base: three short snippets (see worked_example).
Retrieved snippet: the 2024-25 notice with the correct fee.
Answer without RAG: the LLM might give the old fee (₹40,000) because of its knowledge cutoff.
Answer with RAG: the LLM gives the correct current fee (₹45,000) and cites the notice.

sections.heading: ## Key Words to Remember
sections.goal: List the most important terms with one-line definitions.
points: Large Language Model (LLM): an AI model trained on huge text that predicts the next token.
Knowledge cutoff: the date after which the LLM knows nothing.
Hallucination: a confident but wrong or made-up answer.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): a method that retrieves relevant text, adds it to the prompt, then generates the answer.
Chunk: a small piece of a document.
Embedding: a list of numbers that captures the meaning of text.
Embedding model: a tool that turns text into embeddings.
Vector: a list of numbers representing data.
Vector database: a searchable store of vectors.
Semantic search: search by meaning, not just keywords.
Context window: the limited amount of text the model can read at once.
Fine-tuning: training the model further on new examples, which changes its weights.
Retraining: teaching the model again from scratch or continuing training, which changes its weights.

sections.heading: ## Quick Check
sections.goal: Five simple questions to verify understanding.
points: What are the three limits of a plain LLM? (knowledge cutoff, no private data, hallucination)
What does RAG stand for? (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
What are the three question-time steps in order? (retrieve, augment, generate)
Does RAG change the model's weights? (No, the model's weights stay the same.)
Name one benefit and one limitation of RAG. (Benefit: uses fresh/private data. Limitation: answer depends on quality of retrieved chunks.)

sections.heading: ## Summary
sections.goal: Recap the whole lesson in a few sentences.
points: A Large Language Model (LLM) predicts the next token but has a knowledge cutoff, lacks private data, and can hallucinate.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) adds a retrieval step before generation so the LLM uses fresh or private information.
The three steps are retrieve, augment, generate, in that order.
RAG does not retrain the model; it only changes the documents in the knowledge base.
Benefits: up-to-date answers, fewer hallucinations, sources shown. Limitation: the answer is only as good as the retrieved chunks.

quiz.q: What is the full form of RAG?
Which step comes first at question time: retrieve, augment, or generate?
Does RAG change the model's weights?
quiz.a: No, RAG does not change the model's weights. The model stays the same.
A small piece of a document created during the preparation step.

quiz.q: Give one benefit of RAG over fine-tuning.
quiz.a: RAG is cheaper and faster, and knowledge is easy to update by changing documents.
